awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation potential of an artificial intelligence-based violin tutoring system
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact of this I-Corps project is the development of an artificial intelligence (AI) platform to help students learn to play the violin more effectively and affordably. Currently, many students struggle to get private music lessons due to their high cost and limited availability. This platform solves that problem by using regular webcams and microphones, making it easy for anyone to access with a computer. The system provides real-time feedback on how students are playing, helping them improve their posture, bowing, and sound quality. In addition, the technology helps them avoid common mistakes and progress faster while reducing the risk of injuries. Teachers also may benefit from this technology by getting detailed insights into their students' practice habits, allowing them to offer more personalized support. This AI-driven tool may expand access to music education, making it available to more students regardless of where they live or their financial situation. The solution also may appeal to schools, music teachers, and students looking for affordable ways to improve their skills, whether they are learning online or in person. This technology has the potential to keep students more engaged in their musical journey and help them achieve their goals faster.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of advanced artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms that analyze how violin students play by using both visual and audio inputs. The technology evaluates students' posture and bowing technique, providing instant feedback for improvement. Additionally, a unique collection of recorded violin exercises has been digitized to assess students' skills and suggest tailored practice materials. The project aims to enhance online music education by offering personalized tools that help students develop the motor skills essential for playing an instrument. The solution also advances research on how sound and movement interact, creating educational modules customized to individual learners. This project may improve music education and also contribute to scientific knowledge in areas like causal modeling and computational analysis of motion and sound. The data and tools developed may be applied broadly to understand how perception and physical actions are linked, providing valuable insights into the science of learning.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This NSF I-Corps project examined how vAIolin, an artificial intelligence platform for violin practice, could meet the needs of students, parents, and teachers. During the 21-month award period, including a nine-month extension, customer discovery clarified these needs and informed a commercialization strategy and priorities for product development.

The project built on University of Maryland research combining computer vision, sound analysis, and violin pedagogy. The research prototype estimates a violinist’s body position and movements from video and audio and provides posture feedback. The proposed platform uses standard webcams and microphones to support practice between lessons without specialized equipment.

The team conducted 130 customer discovery interviews: 103 during the national I-Corps course and 27 afterward. Participants included violin students, parents, and teachers, alongside music school and program leaders. Interviews examined practice difficulties, desired features, purchasing decisions, and barriers to adoption.

A recurring finding was the gap between what students learn during lessons and what they remember and apply at home. Teachers described substantial effort in documenting assignments, sharing demonstration videos, and revisiting incorrectly practiced material. Parents wanted to help but often lacked musical knowledge or time. Students were not always aware of their posture and movement errors.

These findings broadened product priorities beyond posture feedback. Teachers expressed interest in automated lesson summaries and assignment tracking. Students responded positively to game-like exercises, challenges, and immediate feedback. Teachers were more receptive when vAIolin was presented as supporting their instruction. These responses identified promising features for future development and testing.

Customer discovery identified an initial market of beginner and intermediate violin students, approximately ages 6–16, taking private lessons. Parents emerged as likely purchasers, with teachers as important advisers. Institutional interviews revealed adoption processes often lasting a year or more, alongside openness to pilot studies. The resulting strategy prioritized direct sales to families, supported by teacher recommendations, with institutions as potential pilot partners.

The intellectual contribution of the award was to connect audiovisual movement analysis with evidence about everyday teaching and practice. Findings informed a revised business model and evaluation priorities: posture and playing skills, practice consistency, and teacher time spent preparing summaries and assignments. The team gained training in customer discovery and translating university research into a potential commercial offering.

Broader impacts included involving educators and families in product design and strengthening collaboration between AI researchers and violin pedagogy experts. Affordable guidance using common recording equipment could expand practice support, particularly for families without musical expertise. Consistent feedback may encourage healthier playing habits. These potential benefits require evaluation in future studies.

The project produced documented customer insights, a refined business model, and a plan for development and pilot evaluation. No commercial product was released. Planned next steps include testing prioritized features with teachers and families, evaluating their benefits, and pursuing small-business research grants and other funding for commercialization.
